                                             PROJECT NO. 58000

       RULEMAKING TO UPDATE
                                                           §
      WHOLESALE AND IOU RETAIL                                     PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
                                                           §
    TRANSMISSION COST RECOVERY IN                                           OF TEXAS
                                                           §
          THE ERCOT REGION

TEXAS PUBLIC POLICY FOUNDATION'S COMMENTS ON PROPOSED AMENDMENTS TO
       16 TAC §25.192 AND 16 TAC §25.193 AND PROPOSED NEW 16 TAC §25.252

The Texas Public Policy Foundation (TPPF or the Foundation), through its Life:Powered initiative,
respectfully submits the following comments regarding the PUC’s proposed rule regarding wholesale and
IOU retail transmission cost recovery. TPPF supports the shift to a 12 coincident peak (12CP) method
measured across 30-minute intervals as well as the large load customer tariff. Given the high cost of
future transmission that is directly attributable to the growth of large loads and wind and solar
generation, TPPF continues to recommend that the Commission directly allocate costs to the
resources driving the need for the transmission rather than uplifting the costs to all ratepayers.

Figure 1
Annual Transmission Cost of Service Uplift to an Average Residential Ratepayer, Actual 2022-2024 and
Estimated 2025-2034 (With Line Showing 12CP Adjustment Beginning in 2027)




Note: The numbers in this figure were derived by normalizing the annual TCOS uplift by annual system load (both
historical and projected with a 5% annual increase), multiplying by the average annual residential consumption of 15
MWh, and then multiplying again by 1.4 to account for the fact that residential consumers account for about 34% of
load but pay about 47% of TCOS under the 4CP method. The factor is decreased to 1.25 in 2027 to account for the
residential share dropping to 43% under 12CP, per the forecast from the PUC’s study.1

1
 Public Utility Commission of Texas (PUC). (2026, March 16). Evaluation of transmission cost recovery (draft) in
Project No. 58484. p. 32. https://interchange.puc.texas.gov/Documents/58484_77_1603622.PDF
 Before commenting on other aspects of this rule, it is important to reiterate the drivers of past and future
transmission cost of service (TCOS) uplift charges, as shown in Figure 1. The CREZ lines are still
contributing about $650 million annually to TCOS, about $30 annually per residential ratepayer, and
interconnection costs for generators contribute another $500 million, or $24 per residential ratepayer.2
These costs have remained consistent on a normalized ($/MWh of annual load) basis in recent years, and
if other transmission costs grow in line with demand growth, and not more, the average residential
ratepayer would see their transmission costs remain flat over the next decade, at about $250 per year.

However, future planned transmission is likely to add to these costs substantially. The 765-kV STEP will,
by itself, add an average of about $3 billion annually to TCOS over the 30-plus-year recovery period.3
And more transmission projects that be added following the addition of the Batch Zero loads to ERCOT’s
Regional Transmission plan. The switch to 12CP will slow the increase in transmission costs for the
average residential ratepayer, but even an optimistic projection has TCOS rising $90 per year per
ratepayer by the middle of the next decade instead of $130 per year under the current 4CP method.

Prior to the CREZ lines, new transmission was primarily directed at bringing new dispatchable generation
to Texas cities and reinforcing connectivity near those cities. Residential, commercial, and industrial
consumers all benefitted somewhat equally from the new transmission, and residential consumers drove a
lot of the need given their outsized contribution to peak demand. This is no longer the situation in
ERCOT, with wind, solar, and storage comprising over 90% of new generation and large loads
comprising over 90% of forecasted new demand. Those loads—along with diffuse wind and solar
generation spread across the state—are not usually concentrated near residential loads such that all types
of loads will receive equal benefits from the new builds.

TPPF asserts that the need to connect distant wind and solar generation to new large loads is the
primary driver of the 765-kV STEP and other future transmission projects4 and that a large
portion of the costs of these new projects should be allocated directly to both new intermittent
generation and new large loads. If new demand from large loads was met by local gas generation,
instead of wind and solar spread across the state, the need for cross-state transmission would be sharply
lower. The market design changes needed to shift the generation mix is a question to be addressed in
other contexts, but the drivers of rising transmission costs are simply a matter of physics.

The current rulemaking, in addition to the large load interconnection rule, is taking meaningful steps to
address the demand side of cost allocation, but more must be done to reduce the impact of diffuse wind
and solar generation on transmission costs. To that end, the PUC must reconsider the 765-kV STEP
and find ways to minimize the impact to both landowners and to ratepayers before any cross-state
transmission is given final approval. The PUC should encourage transmission efficient on-site
generation and co-location and ERCOT should be accounting for those types of arrangements in their



2
  Bennett, B. and Piracci, J. (2026, January). The Explosion of Transmission Costs in ERCOT: Causes, Forecasts,
and Policy Solutions. Texas Public Policy Foundation. p. 8. https://www.texaspolicy.com/wp-
content/uploads/2026/01/2026-01-LP-Transmission-Costs-BennettPiracci-updated6-2026.pdf
3
  Bennett & Piracci, 2026, p. 10.
4
  Bennett, B. (2026, June). An Economic Assessment of the 765-kV Strategic Transmission Expansion Plan. Texas
Public Policy Foundation. https://www.texaspolicy.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/2026-05-LP-Strategic-
Transmission-Expansion-Plan-Bennett-combined.pdf
 planning models (which the 765-kV STEP did not do). It should also find methods to encourage more
efficient use of existing transmission infrastructure.

The PUC should also consider adopting a Transmission Reinforcement Payment for new generators,
modeled after the reforms recently adopted by the Alberta Electric System Operator.5 The payment is
designed to be “a function of the suppliers’ proximity to transmission capacity, their technical attributes
and characteristics, and the cost of reinforcing the transmission system.” Such a policy could improve the
development decisions made by generators and ensure that ratepayers are not providing an undue subsidy
to diffuse, intermittent wind and solar generation that demands more transmission. The PUC should also
revisit the generation interconnection cost allowance (16 TAC §25.195), which is currently too high to
provide any meaningful benefits to ratepayers or to improve the siting decisions of generators.6

Those reforms fall outside of the context of this rule, but within this rule, the Commission must do more
than simply modifying the CP method to achieve meaningful relief for residential ratepayers. This is why
TPPF supports the PUC’s proposal to introduce large load interconnection fees. It is critical that the
PUC make some portion of the interconnection fee non-refundable, even if the large load
interconnects at the full capacity that it requested. As the data above shows, it is unlikely that large
loads will pay for their full share of upgrades through TCOS uplift alone. TPPF does not have a
position on whether the fee should be paid in full at the time of interconnection, but it might be reasonable
to allow paying over time given that the purpose is to offset the rate base, which is also paid off over time.

Rather than assigning large loads a fixed interconnection fee with an arbitrary value, the PUC
should consider assigning the cost of specific projects, like any of the proposed 765-kV lines, to new
large loads. Under the current rules, ratepayers are bearing an enormous risk, if large loads do not
interconnect quickly enough to justify the upgrade costs. A direct allocation of costs would provide a
clearer cost-causation balance and reduce that risk. As noted above, an allocation to new generators could
also offset some of the risk to existing ratepayers, but ultimately, some change in the allocation of these
projects to different ratepayers must be done.

For context, the proposed 765-kV lines alone will add roughly $2 billion to the annual TSP revenue
requirements. Even if 20 GW of new large loads interconnect every year, each of them would have to pay
$100,000/MW to offset the full cost of the lines. If only 2 GW connects in a given year, the cost would be
$1,000,000/MW. If large loads only pay a fixed fee, the rest of the rate base is bearing the risk of cost
overruns or of interconnections dropping off and infrastructure being underutilized.

Conversely, the challenge with assigning too many costs up front was made clear in a recent attempt by
the Southwest Power Pool (SPP) to allocate $30 billion in new transmission costs to large loads. It was
reported7 that 122 projects out of 251 total withdrew after the cost allocation numbers were announced.

 The median cost allocated cost of the projects that withdrew was $655,0000/MW, while the median for
the projects that stayed was $244,000/MW. This example is a cautionary tale, but it also shows that many
entities are likely willing to pay more than the $50,000/MW in the PUC’s proposed interconnection
standards rule.8 The PUC should consider a cap in the range of $250,000/MW to ensure that large loads
do not bear an undue amount of risk but allow the fee to float below that amount.

TPPF does not have any responses to staff questions 1, 2, 3, and 6. Below are responses to questions 4
and 5.

Staff Question 4 — Should separate rate treatment be applied to a large computational load, defined as
an entity that is subject to §25.194 of this title (relating to Large Load Interconnection Standards) and in
which 50% or greater of the demand at the site consists of power electronic based load, specifically
computational load, such as data centers and cryptocurrency mining facilities?

While computational loads present a materially different load profile than other large loads and specific
risks due to their higher volatility, TPPF does not support a separate rate treatment for these loads at this
time. In short, there is not enough data to delineate any necessary changes right now. Over time, risks and
costs from computational loads may present themselves that create the need for separate rates, but we
should wait for more data before making that change.

Staff Question 5 — Should the definition for transmission interconnection costs be broadened to include
transmission projects that are recommended at the conclusion of a batch study to serve the
transmission capacity needs of a particular load?

Consistent with the proposal earlier in these comments to assign specific bulk transmission costs to large
loads, TPPF agrees with broadening this definition.

In summary, the need for new long-distance transmission is being driven by the mismatches between the
locations of new large loads and the quantity and type of new generation needed to serve them. Existing
ratepayers, especially residential ratepayers, should not be required to shoulder that risk. A direct
assignment of the cost of new bulk transmission, like what is planned in the 765-kV STEP, to large
loads plus wind and solar generators will place the financial risk where it should lie and will help
keep the rise in residential transmission rates closer to the rate of inflation. Taking this single step
will then free the Commission from dozens of difficult decisions needed to fairly assign other
transmission costs while protecting residential and small commercial ratepayers.

                                                   Sincerely,

                                                   /s/ Brent Bennett
                                                   Brent Bennett, Ph.D.
                                                   Policy Director, Life:Powered
                                                   Texas Public Policy Foundation

                                       PROJECT NO. 58484

                                                   §
 EVALUATION OF TRANSMISSION                                PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
                                                   §
      COST RECOVERY                                                 OF TEXAS
                                                   §

COMMENTS OF THE TEXAS PUBLIC POLICY FOUNDATION: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

 •   Before approving new transmission projects, the Commission and ERCOT should always first
     study alternatives that improve the utilization of existing transmission. In addition, it is
     imperative that market reforms to correct for the overbuilding of wind and solar be implemented
     rapidly to reduce the need for new long-distance transmission.
 •   The lifetime revenue requirement of the 765-kV STEP projects will be almost $100 billion, if
     current cost estimates hold, and add an average of about $3 billion annually to TCOS over the 30-
     plus-year recovery period. If 12CP is applied with no other offsetting factors, the cost of the
     STEP alone, not counting other projects that may follow the Batch Zero loads, would still be
     almost $100 per year for the average residential ratepayer. This is why TPPF supports the
     Commission’s efforts to implement a specific tariff for new large load customers.
 •   TPPF recommends that the Commission allocate the cost of the 765-kV lines, and other bulk
     transmission projects that are designed to meet demand growth from large loads, directly to new
     transmission-voltage customers and to the new wind and solar generators serving them. TPPF’s
     research demonstrates that those entities are almost entirely driving the need for new long-
     distance transmission lines.
 •   Assigning the costs of specific projects, rather than applying a simple flat fee, will enable more
     accurate cost-allocation while also avoiding putting the risk of cost overruns or reduced
     interconnections on existing ratepayers. SPP is already attempting to assign costs in this manner.
     A key lesson learned from that experience is that a cap, perhaps in the range of $250,000/MW,
     might need to be employed to reduce individual project risk and ensure that too many projects do
     not leave the queue after costs are assigned.
 •   TPPF does not support a separate rate treatment for large computational loads at this time, as
     there is not yet enough data to properly assess what additional upgrade costs those loads may
     cause. TPPF does support revisiting this question in the future as the system gains more
     experience dealing with these loads.
 •   TPPF agrees with broadening the definition for transmission interconnection costs to include
     transmission projects that are proposed to serve the needs of specific loads.
 •   TPPF continues to recommend that the PUC lower the generation interconnection cost allowance
     to reduce the burden of those costs to ratepayers and provide a stronger market signal for proper
     siting of new generation.
 •   Furthermore, the Foundation recommends that the Commission consider the Alberta ESO’s
     efforts to implement a non-refundable Transmission Reinforcement Payment for new generators,
     which accounts for the attributes and location of generation when assigning system upgrade costs.
